projects.name: Locations
projects.description: Private Google Timeline explorer with GPS heatmaps, road-matched day views, rail detection, insights, and UK journey cost estimation.

caseStudy.claim: A privacy-first Google Timeline explorer and UK journey cost calculator running on Cloudflare Workers, Neon Postgres with FORCE RLS, and MapLibre GL.
caseStudy.role: Co-creator & full-stack engineer: browser import pipeline, GPS rail detection, MapLibre explorer, and Cloudflare Workers API
caseStudy.problem:
Google moved Timeline data on-device and left users with raw Takeout JSON exports that are awkward to inspect, hard to search across years, and frequently inaccurate on transport modes such as train trips labelled as driving.

Existing self-hosted viewers often require heavy always-on servers or push large location archives through backend APIs without strict database-level tenant isolation.

sections.title: Map-first Timeline explorer and honest GPS routes
sections.body:
Built a responsive MapLibre GL explorer spanning Hotspots (visit-density heatmaps and ranked places), Day View (chronological timelines with playback, sunrise/sunset ticks, and numbered journey badges), Routes, Trips, and Insights.

Instead of trusting raw Google segments blindly, Day View filters GPS spikes, snaps traces onto roads via OSRM map matching only when the route stays within 80 m median distance of recorded fixes, and renders gaps over 10 minutes as faint dashes.
sections.imageAlt: Locations Day View showing Manhattan subway and walking journeys on a dark map, numbered and coloured by transport mode alongside the chronological timeline

sections.title: Browser-side imports and GPS rail detection on a 10 ms Worker budget
sections.body:
To fit within Cloudflare Workers' 10 ms free-tier CPU limit, multi-megabyte Takeout zips and JSON files are unzipped and parsed inside a browser Web Worker using fflate and shared @locations/db/pure modules, then uploaded to Hono in small validated batches.

Static OpenStreetMap z10 rail tiles for Great Britain and Ireland are served straight from CDN assets so the Web Worker can reclassify mislabelled driving legs as train or Underground journeys and snap them onto real railway tracks with zero Worker CPU cost.
sections.imageAlt: Hotspots view displaying a location frequency heatmap alongside ranked places, custom labels, and visit/time totals

sections.title: Multi-tenant isolation and UK Journey cost engine
sections.body:
Every tenant-scoped table enforces two layers of isolation: explicit Drizzle tenant filters combined with Postgres FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY evaluated against a transaction-local app.tenant GUC inside withTenant() on a NOBYPASSRLS database role.

Alongside Timeline exploration, the app integrates Journey cost (/journey-cost), a pure TypeScript engine calculating UK fuel and EV trip costs with PostGIS clean-air zones, tolls, live forecourt prices, and encrypted DVLA plate lookups.
sections.imageAlt: Routes view plotting recorded journeys across months, colour-coded by transport mode with mileage breakdowns

decisions.choice: Parse Takeout archives and compute statistics in a browser Web Worker
decisions.why: Parsing a 15 MB Timeline export takes ~200 ms and computing analytics ~230 ms, exceeding Cloudflare Workers' 10 ms free-tier CPU cap.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires paged aggregate rebuilds and resumable batch uploads from the client, in exchange for near-zero server CPU usage and unrestricted export sizes.

decisions.choice: Combine Drizzle tenant filters with Postgres FORCE RLS and a NOBYPASSRLS role
decisions.why: Precise location histories and encrypted vehicle registration plates are high-sensitivity PII where a single missed WHERE clause would be unacceptable.
decisions.tradeoff: Every authenticated request runs inside an explicit transaction via withTenant(), and external OSRM/Nominatim calls must be deferred until after commit.

decisions.choice: Ship static z10 OSM rail tiles as CDN assets for client-side rail matching
decisions.why: Allows reliable reclassification and track-snapping of mislabelled train rides without adding Worker subrequests, database load, or paid rail APIs.
decisions.tradeoff: Detailed railway track snapping covers Great Britain, the Isle of Man, and Ireland only (falling back to speed heuristics elsewhere) and uses manual tile rebuilds.

caseStudy.outcome:
Live in production at locations.aden.website with an interactive, read-only public demo account (Manhattan and Boston sample landmarks) and full MIT-licensed self-hosting support.

Includes Better Auth (email/password, OTP, magic link, optional Google OAuth), optional Stripe billing and customer portal, GDPR ZIP/GPX/GeoJSON exports, 30 dark/light colour moods, and a staff ops panel.

projects.name: Finance
projects.description: A private UK personal finance ledger for savings, spending, credit, payroll, and tax, backed by Cloudflare Workers and Neon Postgres.

caseStudy.claim: A single-origin UK personal finance ledger uniting savings, debt, bills, payroll, and tax with zero floating-point math and database-level row security.
caseStudy.role: Sole designer and engineer — full-stack architecture, financial mathematics, database RLS, Cloudflare Worker API, and React 19 web app
caseStudy.problem:
Personal finance tracking often falls into two extremes: commercial applications that harvest bank credentials and sell user data, or fragile spreadsheets plagued by manual formula errors, untracked transaction gaps, and floating-point rounding bugs.

Managing UK-specific financial realities—such as ISA annual subscription limits across standard and flexible accounts, Personal Savings Allowance (PSA) brackets, Scottish vs. UK tax bands, student loan deductions across Plans 1/2/4/Postgrad, and 0% credit card promotional expirations—requires domain-accurate calculations that generic trackers completely ignore.

A dependable personal ledger must treat money with uncompromising mathematical precision, guarantee tenant privacy at the database engine level, and remain instantaneous without relying on brittle third-party scraping.

sections.title: Exact financial ledger and UK tax engine
sections.body:
Built a zero-floating-point financial calculation engine where every monetary figure is stored in integer pence and every interest rate in integer basis points (525 = 5.25% AER). All calendar math is strictly anchored to the Europe/London timezone and the UK tax year (6 April to 5 April).

The engine models nuanced UK rules out of the box: flexible ISA withdrawal and replacement tracking, Personal Savings Allowance thresholds based on total estimated income, Lifetime ISA (LISA) penalty rules, student loan repayment deductions across all UK plans, and dual-source payroll with custom pension relief.
sections.imageAlt: Finance dashboard showing net worth, account balances, savings allowance progress, and upcoming bills.

sections.title: Single-origin Cloudflare Worker with Neon RLS
sections.body:
Architected a single-origin deployment on a Cloudflare Worker that serves the compiled React 19 SPA while routing /api/* directly to a Hono REST API. Because the web client and API share an identical origin, authentication cookies remain strict first-party httpOnly with SameSite=Lax, completely eliminating cross-origin preflight requests (CORS) and token storage in browser storage.

Database multitenancy is enforced through Neon Postgres Row-Level Security (RLS). Every query runs under a restricted finance_app role (NOBYPASSRLS), scoped dynamically to app.user_id. Even raw SQL queries executed directly in the database cannot leak data between users without explicit tenant configuration.
sections.imageAlt: Finance accounts spreadsheet view and credit card balance transfer management interface.

sections.title: Passwordless authentication, passkeys, and daily 1p challenges
sections.body:
Implemented a frictionless, passwordless authentication flow with 6-digit email codes and magic links powered by Better Auth and Resend, complemented by WebAuthn passkeys for instant biometric login. Authentication endpoints are rate-limited via Cloudflare Workers KV, and a generic confirmation message prevents user enumeration.

Built interactive features including opt-in 364/365-day Daily 1p Savings Challenges that deterministically calculate and catch up micro-deposits whenever the user opens the app, and version 5 atomic backup/restore allowing users to export full database records or restore across migrations with verified relational integrity.
sections.imageAlt: Account activity ledger displaying statement checkpoints, linked transfers, and daily penny savings challenge catch-ups.

decisions.choice: Integer pence and basis points over standard floats or decimals
decisions.why: Floating-point arithmetic introduces insidious rounding inaccuracies over time (e.g. 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3). By enforcing minor currency units (pence) and basis points across shared Zod schemas, database columns, and client state, rounding is strictly controlled and occurs only at defined presentation boundaries.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires explicit conversion helpers whenever accepting user input or rendering formatted currency strings in UI components.

decisions.choice: Single-origin Worker proxying over decoupled web and API origins
decisions.why: Bundling static Vite assets directly into Cloudflare Workers with Hono intercepting /api/* guarantees zero-CORS latency and enables first-party httpOnly session cookies without third-party cookie restrictions or browser blocking.
decisions.tradeoff: Asset builds and API deployments are coupled in a single Worker deployment pipeline, requiring end-to-end atomic builds.

decisions.choice: Postgres Row-Level Security (RLS) over application-level WHERE clauses
decisions.why: Relying solely on developers remembering WHERE user_id = ? in every ORM query risks silent security leaks during joins, updates, or bulk restores. Neon Postgres RLS with a NOBYPASSRLS application role provides defense-in-depth at the database kernel.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires setting connection-level session variables (SET LOCAL app.user_id) on each pooled transaction and specialized configuration for local testing.

decisions.choice: Statement-driven balance snapshots over raw event-sourcing balance accumulation
decisions.why: In real-world banking, user transaction logs often suffer from gaps, pending authorizations, or untracked fees. Treating user-entered statement snapshots as authoritative end-of-day anchors and layering active movements between statements ensures data always agrees with bank reality.
decisions.tradeoff: Ledger calculations must detect and handle gaps between statements and opening balances rather than relying on a continuous event stream.

caseStudy.outcome:
The application is deployed in production at https://finance.humza.website, operating as a fully functional, private personal finance ledger. Users can register via passwordless email authentication, attach WebAuthn passkeys, track all accounts/debts/investments, import Emma/Monzo CSVs, reconcile recurring subscriptions, calculate take-home payroll and tax pots, and export full tax-year reports.

Automated morning email reminders (via cron) are intentionally disabled in the current Cloudflare Worker configuration, though the underlying reminder logic and on-demand test dispatch remain fully implemented in Settings. Open Banking API sync was researched (docs/decisions/2026-10-01-open-banking-ais.md) and consciously deferred in favor of statement snapshots and CSV imports.

projects.name: InvoiceUI
projects.description: Private invoicing workspace with real-time preview, atomic numbering, pure edge PDF compilation, and payment tracking.

caseStudy.claim: Private invoicing workspace with instant vector PDFs, decimal-safe accounting, and immutable snapshots.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer - edge architecture, UI design system, PDF compilation engine, and deployment
caseStudy.problem:
Commercial invoicing tools like QuickBooks, FreshBooks, and Xero are burdened with feature bloat, escalating subscription costs, and intrusive third-party financial tracking. Most suffer from floating-point rounding bugs in tax calculations, fragile browser-print dialogs that destroy document page breaks, and arbitrary limits on basic customizations.

Freelance and client work demands a private, distraction-free tool that creates invoices as fast as a text document, compiles pixel-perfect downloadable PDFs at the edge, and guarantees that historical issued invoices remain permanently immutable even when business addresses or catalogue rates evolve.

sections.title: Two-Column Split Composer with Real-Time Live Preview
sections.body:
Engineered an interactive split-view interface pairing a comprehensive form editor with an instant, reactive document preview. As the owner updates line items, payment terms, or client selections, the state synchronizes smoothly with debounced local recovery storage and the edge API.

Version check safeguards prevent cross-device write conflicts, while atomic sequencing guarantees that once an invoice is issued, its numbering and metadata are permanently locked against catalogue drift.
sections.imageAlt: InvoiceUI split composer showing dark mode editor controls alongside live invoice preview

sections.title: Serverless Vector PDF Compilation at the Edge
sections.body:
Bypassed heavy, timeout-prone headless browser rendering by compiling pure vector PDFs directly inside the Cloudflare Worker using pdf-lib and fontkit. The edge renderer supports three distinct typographical templates (Studio, Minimal, and Classic) with brand accents, embedded logos, and dynamic page-budgeting for long descriptions.

Issued PDFs are archived directly into private Cloudflare R2 storage, enabling instant downloads, secure email attachments via Resend, and unguessable tokenized share links.
sections.imageAlt: Generated vector PDF invoice document preview with itemized rates and breakdown summary

sections.title: Tactile Motion System and Financial Health Ledger
sections.body: Designed a cohesive financial dashboard featuring multi-currency receivables, ageing debt buckets (1-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91+ days), and partial payment reconciliation. The interface combines all five mandated modern UI libraries (shadcn/ui, Motion, Magic UI, React Bits, and Animate UI) to deliver tactile button depression, spring-animated modals, and animated NumberTicker summaries without sacrificing accessibility.
sections.imageAlt: InvoiceUI mobile dashboard displaying outstanding balances, receivables, and invoice status filters

decisions.choice: Single Cloudflare Worker for SPA assets and Hono API
decisions.why: Eliminated CORS latency and secondary hosting infrastructure by routing both static client assets and backend edge API endpoints through one unified Worker on a custom domain.
decisions.tradeoff: Client and server code must adhere to Cloudflare Worker edge execution constraints and bundle size budgets.

decisions.choice: Pure JavaScript pdf-lib rendering over Headless Chrome
decisions.why: Avoided heavy, slow-booting browser containers that exceed edge serverless memory limits, achieving sub-100ms document generation entirely in memory.
decisions.tradeoff: Document layouts, pagination breaks, and text wrapping had to be implemented mathematically rather than relying on browser CSS layout engines.

decisions.choice: Decimal.js fixed-point arithmetic and copy-by-value snapshots
decisions.why: Prevented IEEE-754 floating-point cent errors in multi-tier tax and discount calculations, while ensuring issued invoices never change if reusable client or service records are updated.
decisions.tradeoff: Required strict data validation and conversion layers across API boundaries.

caseStudy.outcome:
Shipped and deployed live to production at invoiceui.humza.website as a verified private invoicing workspace. Running entirely within free tiers across Cloudflare Workers, Neon PostgreSQL, Cloudflare R2, and Resend.

The system has 71 automated tests verifying passwordless owner authentication, multi-currency accounting, idempotent email dispatch, and full workspace JSON/ZIP exports with disaster recovery.

projects.name: 26 Birthday Quiz
projects.description: Real-time multiplayer birthday party game for 80 phones and a projector — with live sabotage trolls, Stockfish chess, and 3D kart racing.

caseStudy.claim: A real-time multiplayer party game built for an 80-guest 26th birthday — pairing mobile phone controllers with a projector stage, live sabotage trolls, Stockfish chess, and 3D kart racing.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — Durable Object room engine, 10+ game mechanics, Three.js kart racer, operator console, and deploy
caseStudy.problem:
Off-the-shelf party quiz tools break down when you want custom round mechanics, live audience sabotage, projector-synchronised photo walls, and a 3D racing finale under unreliable venue Wi-Fi. Typical quiz apps either lock content behind rigid templates, leak answer keys to the client, or lose room state when mobile browsers sleep and reconnect mid-round.

I built a bespoke party platform where a presenter drives the big screen, an operator cues and moderates the show from a live desk, and up to 80 guests play individually on their own phones with zero app installs or accounts.

sections.title: Authoritative rooms on Durable Objects and WebSockets
sections.body:
Each party room runs inside a single SQLite-backed Cloudflare Durable Object (PartyRoom) served by the same Hono Worker that hosts the React app. Phones send intents over one reconnecting WebSocket with idempotent request receipts, while the server validates deadlines, persists accepted actions to SQLite before acknowledging, and drives phase changes via a single durable alarm scheduler.

Guest snapshots intentionally strip answer keys, presenter notes, and host controls. Post-game archiving to Neon Postgres and optional Resend email recaps run strictly outside the live tap path.
sections.imageAlt: Guest controller with live question and countdown timer.

sections.title: Bespoke rounds from Wordle to Three.js kart racing
sections.body:
The birthday pack spans 53 ordered rounds across photo trivia, partial-credit multi-select, consensus sliders, tap ranking, knockout text ballots, push-your-luck escalations, Leaflet map guessing, a 5-letter Wordle round, simultaneous 1-minute chess against in-browser Stockfish 19 WASM, and a 3D Three.js kart Grand Prix.

To keep 80 phones smooth on venue Wi-Fi, kart races use trusted device-recorded active elapsed times with ordered lap splits and local rollback prediction while the room owns admission and standings. Heavy engines (Three.js, Stockfish, and /admin) are lazy-loaded to keep the initial join bundle fast.
sections.imageAlt: Custom question design with A/B presentation and live voting interface.

sections.title: Theme system and visual identity
sections.body:
Built a palette-plus-skin theme engine with 79 switchable party themes, from '26 basic' (warm coral and gold) to Persona references and nostalgia palettes. Each theme supplies 12 colour roles, a typeface treatment, motion presets, and optional background scenes (spotlights, synthwave grids, stars, doodles).

Skins add identity markers: Persona 5 shards, kart racing motifs, birthday candle lighting. All animations respect reduced-motion preferences.
sections.imageAlt: Theme picker showing multiple party palettes and scene backgrounds.

sections.title: Live sabotage trolls and a rehearsal-ready operator desk
sections.body:
From round two onward, guests spend cooldown-gated tokens across 49 troll gags—warping a rival's phone UI, firing projector stings, or applying deterministic score modifiers (double, steal, robin-hood, share) during reveal.

Every feature ships with a matching /admin view so the host can cue rounds, pair a presenter phone, moderate uploaded photos, issue one-time phone transfer codes, and rehearse the full show against up to 100 simulated WebSocket bots.
sections.imageAlt: Host control panel with real-time phase controls and player management.

decisions.choice: One SQLite-backed Durable Object per room instead of external DB calls during play
decisions.why: Colocating WebSocket hibernation, round state, receipts, and a single alarm scheduler inside PartyRoom avoids cross-region latency during 80-phone bursts and survives socket drops.
decisions.tradeoff: Deploying mid-game restarts active rooms and drops connections, and 80-player kart races require Cloudflare Workers Paid to stay within Durable Object SQLite row limits.

decisions.choice: Device-recorded kart lap timing with local rollback prediction
decisions.why: Early 80-bot staging rehearsals showed that streaming every steering tick through the Durable Object overloaded the alarm loop and triggered reconnect storms.
decisions.tradeoff: Relies on each phone's monotonic active timer for race finish durations instead of pure server-tick physics—trading strict anti-cheat for responsive 60fps mobile racing among friends.

decisions.choice: Versioned TypeScript question packs instead of a runtime CMS
decisions.why: Keeping all 59 catalogued rounds in server-only TypeScript lets preflight checks verify media, timers, and answer shapes while ensuring secrets never enter the client bundle.
decisions.tradeoff: Content changes require a code deploy, though hosts can still reorder and freeze the active running order from /admin prior to starting a game.

caseStudy.outcome:
26.humza.website shipped to production at https://26.humza.website for Humza's 26th birthday on 21 November 2026, with standalone /kart and /chess solo practice, synced /host projector views, live /admin operator controls, and immutable Neon-backed /r/:gameId archive pages.

Public visitors without a room code can browse the landing page and play solo kart or chess immediately, while live quiz rooms remain gated by room codes and allow-listed administrator sign-in.

projects.name: Specimen Archive
projects.description: A catalogue of 651 portable motion specimens: live previews, one-click recreation prompts, and a playground for exporting new ones.

caseStudy.claim: 651 motion specimens, each archived with its source, its contract, and a prompt that rebuilds it anywhere.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — catalogue UX and design system, sandboxed preview harness, 651-specimen registry, prompt builder, playground editor with zip export, and the Cloudflare Pages deploy pipeline.
caseStudy.problem:
Motion detail is the first thing lost between projects. A hover, a transition, a completion burst gets built once in one codebase, then survives only as a screen recording or a Slack link — not as something a future agent or teammate can re-run and re-use. Screenshots cannot be pasted into a new repo, and "make it feel like the reference" is not a specification.

The second problem is mechanical. These artifacts are arbitrary CSS with global class names, loud palettes, and infinite loops. They cannot share a document with the site chrome: one * { } reset or a .track collision and the host page eats itself. The archive had to isolate styling completely without editing a single line of the specimen.

sections.title: Sandboxed previews that never touch the chrome
sections.body:
Every preview renders inside an iframe srcdoc with sandbox="allow-scripts" and nothing else. That one decision buys true style isolation, so specimen CSS stays verbatim and portable instead of scoped, renamed, or restyled. Playback, reduced-motion emulation, viewport, and background all run against the frame's own document.

The frame is also the control surface: restart and replay are postMessage commands, and playback rate is applied through document.getAnimations() inside the sandbox. Because the frame has no same-origin access, the harness cannot reach in and fix a specimen — which is exactly the property that keeps copied code honest.
sections.imageAlt: The catalogue: filter rails for kind, tech, scope, intensity and inspiration above a grid of specimen plates, each with a live preview.

sections.title: A prompt builder instead of a screenshot
sections.body:
buildPrompt(specimen, mode) produces three clipboard payloads per specimen: the full recreation prompt, code only, and contract only. The full prompt is written for an agent that has never heard of this site: intent, dependencies, host requirements, markup, styles, behaviour, the JSON contract, integration steps, and observable acceptance criteria ("marquee loops with no visible seam", not "looks good").

Nothing in the generated text describes the archive. That constraint is what makes the output portable — the receiving agent gets the artifact, not the museum label.
sections.imageAlt: A specimen detail page: sandboxed preview with viewport, background, reduced-motion and playback controls, beside tabbed Spec, Markup, Styles, Contract and Prompt source.

sections.title: A playground that closes the loop
sections.body:
/playground is a split view: a CodeMirror 6 editor (HTML/CSS/JS tabs) on the left, the same sandboxed harness on the right, with the shared control strip underneath — 320/360/768/full viewport, four backgrounds, three reduced-motion modes, pause and 0.25×–2× playback, restart. Drafts debounce to localStorage; Share compresses a draft into the URL hash with lz-string, so a link is inert but reproducible, with no backend involved.

Export specimen generates the real folder — demo.html, demo.css, optional demo.js, a filled entry.ts, a spec.md scaffold, and a contract.json derived from what it can read (angles, durations, colours found in the CSS) with TODO markers for the rest — and downloads it as a zip. That export path is why the catalogue reached 651 entries instead of stalling at a dozen.
sections.imageAlt: The playground: CodeMirror HTML editor for a forked calling-card specimen, live sandboxed preview, control strip, and Export specimen.

decisions.choice: Sandboxed srcdoc iframes instead of scoped CSS
decisions.why: The specimens are hostile by design — global selectors, clashing palettes, infinite animation — and must stay copy-paste-identical to what runs. Isolation at the document boundary is the only version that keeps the CSS unedited.
decisions.tradeoff: No host access to the frame document, so every control has to be a postMessage protocol, and cross-frame state such as scroll, theme, or storage is deliberately impossible.

decisions.choice: Explicit sharded registry with metadata-only entries
decisions.why: 651 entries in one import list is unmaintainable and a bundle hazard. Entries carry metadata and a loadPayload thunk; HTML, CSS, JS, spec and contract load only when a detail page or prompt needs them. Shards per franchise plus a canonical order.ts keep ref numbering deterministic, with no import.meta.glob.
decisions.tradeoff: Adding a specimen is a manual registration step, mitigated by the spec:ship scaffolder and a spec:check validator, and franchise shards must be kept in sync by hand.

decisions.choice: Monochrome chrome with a single reserved accent
decisions.why: The content is maximal; the frame must be quiet or the page becomes unusable. A parts-catalogue register — numbered refs, hairline rules, mono metadata — lets a bright caution tape sit two inches from the UI without the UI competing. Verdigris is reserved for focus, active state, and copy confirmation.
decisions.tradeoff: The brand is deliberately colourless, so identity has to come from typography, density, and the specimens themselves.

decisions.choice: Static site with content in git, no backend
decisions.why: A specimen is files — diffable, lintable, copyable. Keeping the catalogue as repo content means every published artifact is reviewable in a pull request, and the whole site is a static Cloudflare Pages deploy with no runtime to secure or pay for.
decisions.tradeoff: No accounts, no server-side search, no saved collections, no analytics; publishing requires a commit.

caseStudy.outcome:
Live at https://playground.humza-butt.space — 651 specimens across 22 franchise families, browsable by kind, tech, scope, intensity and inspiration, with four preview densities and per-plate playback. Every entry can be copied out as a prompt or opened in the playground, and new specimens can be authored and exported in the browser. The repo is public and deploys automatically from main.

Known edges: there is no backend, so no accounts, saved collections, or server-side search; three scaffolded folders are not yet registered; and a share link is a snapshot, not a live document. A 20-second launch video exists but is not embedded on the site.

projects.name: Encore
projects.description: A daily puzzle arcade for players who want more than one round, with endless practice, curated catalogues, and past boards to replay.

caseStudy.claim: Encore turns a once-a-day puzzle into something you can practise, revisit, and get better at.
caseStudy.role: Project creator and engineer across puzzle generation, web, API, and deployment.

metrics.label: Play modes for the original grid games

caseStudy.problem:
A daily puzzle gives players one shared challenge. After a solve, players who want to practise need fresh boards, and anyone who missed a day needs a way back to that day's puzzle. Encore brings both options into the same game.

That creates a technical constraint. A dated board has to stay recognisable after the generator changes, and a newly generated logic board has to be playable with exactly one solution.

sections.title: A puzzle arcade with room to practise
sections.body: I built a shared home for daily games, starting with Stitch, Quilt, and Weave. Each original grid game has a daily board, a calendar of past challenges, a curated catalogue, and a practice mode for generating more boards.
sections.imageAlt: Encore game picker showing Stitch, Quilt, and Weave, with links for daily play, practice, and past puzzles.

sections.title: A generator that can replay the same board
sections.body: I built a TypeScript engine that generates a board from a seed and a pinned generator version. A daily seed identifies the game, UTC date, and difficulty. Practice uses its own seed tokens, and the same seed and version reproduce the same board wherever it is generated. For the original grid games, a solver rejects candidates without exactly one solution.
sections.imageAlt: Medium Stitch daily puzzle with numbered checkpoints and walls on a six-by-six grid.

sections.title: Archives and progress across visits
sections.body: I built an archive that opens a dated challenge after the daily rollover. It can rebuild recent boards from their seeds when the API is unavailable. Guest boards and catalogue progress persist in the browser. Signed-in players can sync in-progress boards and catalogue clears through the same-origin Worker API, with Neon PostgreSQL row-level policies isolating player data.
sections.imageAlt: Stitch archive with a 12-week activity grid, a date picker, and recent puzzles available offline.

decisions.choice: Versioned, seeded grid generation
decisions.why: Reproduce dated boards and generate new practice puzzles from compact identifiers.
decisions.tradeoff: Shipped generator logic must stay reproducible when new versions are added.

decisions.choice: One Worker for SPA and API
decisions.why: Ship static assets and the same-origin API together, with one canonical origin per environment.
decisions.tradeoff: Frontend and API deployment and rollback share a release unit.

decisions.choice: Forced row-level security in PostgreSQL
decisions.why: Put player data isolation in the database and check it in CI.
decisions.tradeoff: Each schema change adds policy work and tests for access boundaries.

caseStudy.outcome: Encore is live with no-account play, daily and archived challenges, catalogues, and practice. The original grid games now sit alongside additional puzzle families, including letter guessing and geography. The build includes account progress sync, and the production account flag is enabled. Stripe Premium is disabled in production.

projects.name: Baseer Portfolio
projects.description: Marketing CV site for Baseer with a freeform visual CMS, first-party analytics, and sector case studies.

caseStudy.claim: Marketing CV site for Baseer with a freeform visual CMS, first-party analytics, and sector case studies.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — CMS, Worker API, analytics, and marketing surfaces

metrics.label: Worker hosting site, CMS, and analytics

caseStudy.problem:
A CV site is only useful if its owner can restyle it without a developer, and template builders lock content into fixed slots.

Baseer needed sector case studies he could rearrange freely, plus visitor insight without handing traffic data to a third-party tracker.

sections.title: Marketing site and sector case studies
sections.body:
A CV-led landing page with sector case studies, each editable as freeform content rather than a fixed template field.

Motion and layout are tuned for a marketing read rather than a document dump.
sections.imageAlt: Baseer portfolio landing page with headline and sector navigation

sections.title: Freeform CMS and first-party analytics
sections.body:
Better Auth gates a visual CMS that writes to Neon Postgres through Drizzle, with media on R2.

Analytics are collected by the same Worker, so visitor data never leaves the site’s own domain.
sections.imageAlt: Baseer portfolio case-study content section further down the page

decisions.choice: Freeform visual CMS over a fixed template
decisions.why: The owner edits layout and copy directly instead of filing change requests.
decisions.tradeoff: More validation and migration work than a fixed set of content fields.

decisions.choice: First-party analytics inside the same Worker
decisions.why: Keeps visitor data on the site’s own domain and avoids loading a third-party tracker.
decisions.tradeoff: Reporting, retention, and dashboards are ours to build and maintain.

decisions.choice: Neon Postgres with Drizzle behind Hono
decisions.why: Content and analytics share one typed relational schema with cheap edge reads.
decisions.tradeoff: Connection handling from Workers needs deliberate pooling.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at baseer.co.uk: marketing site, sector case studies, R2-backed media, a Better Auth-protected visual CMS, and first-party analytics on a single Cloudflare deploy.

projects.name: Docket
projects.description: Personal job-application tracker with Kanban, list, stats, docs, reminders, and email alerts—built for a single owner, no login.

caseStudy.claim: Personal job-application tracker with Kanban, list, stats, docs, reminders, and email alerts—built for a single owner, no login.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — product, API, and infrastructure
caseStudy.timeline: 2026 · in daily use, live at jobtracker.humza-butt.space

metrics.label: tracker surfaces: Kanban, list, stats, docs, reminders

caseStudy.problem:
A spreadsheet of applications loses the timeline: which stage each role is at, which CV version was sent, and when a follow-up is due.

Docket has exactly one user, so accounts, tenancy, and onboarding would have been pure overhead on top of the tracking itself.

sections.title: Kanban and list tracking
sections.body:

projects.name: Tetris
projects.description: A polished, dependency-free Tetris with SRS wall kicks, 7-bag randomizer, T-spins, combo scoring, and a keyboard-first canvas UI.

caseStudy.claim: A complete, guideline-accurate Tetris that ships as three static files and zero dependencies.
caseStudy.role: Sole engineer — mechanics, scoring, input, rendering, audio, responsive UI, and deployment.
caseStudy.problem:
It is easy to find browser Tetris implementations that look right but cut corners on the mechanics that make the game feel fair — SRS wall kicks, 180° rotation, lock delay, T-spin detection, back-to-back bonuses — or that pull in a framework and build pipeline for what is fundamentally a canvas and an input loop.

I wanted a version that loads instantly, can be opened from a static folder, and still feels like a modern guideline game. That meant implementing the rules properly, then spending the remaining effort on input timing, responsive layout, and feedback instead of tooling.

sections.title: Guideline mechanics, not a lookalike
sections.body:
The engine implements SRS rotation with separate I-piece and JLSTZ kick tables, plus a 180° kick table. A 7-bag randomizer feeds the hold queue and a five-piece preview. Pieces get a ghost projection, a 500 ms lock delay with up to 15 resets, and T-spin detection using the three-corner rule.

Scoring covers singles through tetrises, T-spins, back-to-back bonuses, and combo chains. Line clears flash, score callouts float over the board, and level-ups accelerate gravity from 1,000 ms per row down to a 48 ms floor.
sections.imageAlt: Mid-game Tetris board with a colorful stack, ghost piece, score and level HUD, and the five-piece next queue.

sections.title: Three static files and a canvas
sections.body:
The playfield is one canvas, sized from its container and capped at 2.5× device pixel ratio so it stays sharp without exploding the backing store. Hold and next previews use small dedicated canvases. A ResizeObserver plus a window-resize handler rebuild the layout, and the requestAnimationFrame loop clamps delta time to 50 ms so a tab stall does not teleport pieces.

There is no framework, bundler, or runtime dependency. public/index.html, public/styles.css, and public/game.js are the whole app; wrangler deploy publishes that folder to Cloudflare's edge.
sections.imageAlt: Tetris start screen with hold panel, score/best/level/lines stats, next queue, and a keyboard controls reference.

decisions.choice: Vanilla JS in one IIFE, with no build step
decisions.why: The whole game is a state machine, a render loop, and an input map. A framework would add a toolchain and a bundle for no runtime benefit, and static files can be opened locally or served by any host.
decisions.tradeoff: No type checking, component model, or tree-shaking; the file is 1,208 lines and every change is manual.

decisions.choice: Canvas 2D for the board and previews
decisions.why: A 10 × 20 grid with effects and a ghost piece redraws cheaply, and canvas keeps the DOM small. DPR-aware sizing capped at 2.5× keeps it crisp on high-density screens.
decisions.tradeoff: Everything is coordinate math and manual redraw; board cells are not DOM nodes, so accessibility relies on ARIA labels and the separate HUD.

decisions.choice: Time-based DAS/ARR instead of OS key repeat
decisions.why: OS key-repeat rates vary and feel inconsistent. Tracking key state and stepping movement against delta time gives the same 160 ms delay / 42 ms repeat feel in every browser.
decisions.tradeoff: More input state to manage, including releases on blur/tab-hide and a separate pointer-repeat path for touch controls.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at tetris.humza.website on Cloudflare Workers static assets, playable in a desktop or mobile browser with no account, install, or backend. The game ships with the full guideline mechanics, synthesized audio, a local best score, and on-screen controls on small screens. Still off: there is no automated test suite or CI, no online leaderboard or cross-device sync, and browser support has been checked manually rather than across a formal matrix.

projects.name: Pokémon Battle Simulator
projects.description: A web tool for Pokémon fans to run automated battles, compare one-on-one matchup grids, and build teams for trainer tournaments.

caseStudy.claim: Run automated Pokémon battles and see how entire pools of Pokémon match up.
caseStudy.role: Full-stack developer for the web edition — React interface, Flask integration, matchup tooling, accounts, and deployment.
caseStudy.problem:
The original simulator let players run large batches of Pokémon Showdown battles from the command line. Comparing a new team or a pool of Pokémon meant editing input files, running scripts, and reviewing the exported results separately.

I built a browser workflow so Pokémon fans could set up their own comparisons, inspect outcomes, and revisit previous runs.

sections.title: Configure a battle or a whole pool
sections.body:
The matchup simulator runs one-on-one battles between two selected Pokémon or all unique pairings in a filtered pool. Filters cover traits such as type, region, evolution stage, and base stat total. Players can inspect the selected sets, use Smogon presets, or provide custom movesets.

Full, quick, and sampled strategies run battles through Pokémon Showdown. A heuristic strategy estimates matchups using type effectiveness and base stats.
sections.imageAlt: Matrix setup with full evolution, Fire and Water types, and Kanto selected beside the battle settings.

sections.title: Read and revisit the results
sections.body: The matchup workspace turns run outputs into win-rate charts, a heatmap, and a searchable table. JSON and CSV exports let players keep the raw results. A separate upload view reads results locally in the browser, while signed-in users can save runs to their account.
sections.imageAlt: Upload Results screen showing a wins bar chart and matchup table for a sample run.

sections.title: Build teams for trainer tournaments
sections.body: The Team Builder uses Pokédex data for species, abilities, items, and moves. Players can set EVs and IVs, export Showdown-format builds to the editor, and use the tournament workspace to build battles, run simulations, and produce PNG and CSV reports.
sections.imageAlt: Tournament Team Builder with Charizard selected and its base stats, EVs, IVs, and moveset controls visible.

decisions.choice: Wrap Pokémon Showdown with Flask and Python
decisions.why: The existing battle engine and batch scripts could keep running while the web app handled configuration, progress, and downloads.
decisions.tradeoff: The backend has to build and run both Python and Node.js components and manage long-running jobs.

decisions.choice: Offer four matchup strategies
decisions.why: The number of unique pairings rises quickly with the pool size, so players can choose how much computation to spend.
decisions.tradeoff: Quick runs have fewer trials, sampled runs skip pairings, and heuristic results are estimates based on type and stats.

decisions.choice: Use Supabase with source-data fallbacks
decisions.why: Persist user configurations and saved results, and serve cached dex records and Smogon sets when available.
decisions.tradeoff: The app has to maintain data imports and fallback paths for local dex files and remotely fetched sets.

decisions.choice: Deploy the frontend and simulation API separately
decisions.why: Serve the React interface from Netlify while running Python and Node.js simulation jobs on Render.
decisions.tradeoff: The deployment needs coordination between the frontend’s API URL, allowed origins, and authentication redirects.

caseStudy.outcome: The public web edition offers matchup setup, team building, a Pokédex, and browser-based analysis of imported results. Running simulations on the server and saving them to an account require sign-in. The command-line workflow is still available in the public repository.

caseStudy.role: Lead engineer — Next.js 16 architecture, Cloudflare Workers migration, interactive UI, forms, and automated QA
caseStudy.problem:
LifeSmart Education Ltd runs gamified financial education programmes across UK schools, corporate and public-sector partners (including SP ZeroFinance and the Bank of England), and community charities—but its legacy Squarespace site could not deliver bespoke interactive showcases, strict privacy controls, or edge performance.

The rebuild had to communicate three distinct offerings without a CMS or database, preserve high-authority inbound links from institutional partners, collect zero student data across all enquiry flows, and remain completely usable before hydration or with JavaScript disabled.

sections.title: Typed content architecture & v12 design system
sections.body:
Built on Next.js 16 App Router and Tailwind CSS v4, the site stores all marketing copy, impact metrics, FAQs, and media dimensions in strict TypeScript modules rather than a headless CMS. Design tokens—colours, fluid display scales, and a constrained 3-duration/3-curve motion vocabulary—are enforced centrally in CSS and TypeScript.

Following an October v10/v12 redesign pass, shared primitives power the 18 core marketing and resource pages, with retired prototype stylesheets isolated so live routes never download unused CSS.
sections.imageAlt: LifeSmart homepage dark hero featuring rotating audience contexts, live classroom photography, and an interactive scorecard preview.

sections.title: Interactive money-moment previews & disciplined motion
sections.body:
To show rather than tell how LifeSmart teaches money, the homepage pairs server-rendered classroom race illustrations and learning-tool previews with lightweight interactive components under LazyMotion strict mode. Visitors can roll a 3D-styled dice control to step through six financial-literacy scenarios, toggle light and dark top surfaces, or scroll through a viewport-aware sticky card deck.

Every interaction degrades cleanly: sticky cards collapse into normal document flow on short viewports and mobile, touch devices keep the hero context static, and native disclosure and radio controls keep navigation, research cards, and FAQ filters functional without JavaScript.
sections.imageAlt: Interactive Money Moments dice card and the three-card BuildStack overview for schools, organisations, and communities.

sections.title: Zero-JS-safe forms, security headers, & Workers edge cutover
sections.body:
Enquiry, school-eligibility, and registration forms run through four Next.js Server Actions backed by Resend, Cloudflare Workers IP rate limiting (5 submissions per 60 seconds), honeypot trapping, and optional Turnstile verification. All fields use native HTML validation and inline accessible error states before hydration.

For deployment on Cloudflare Workers via @opennextjs/cloudflare, prerendered pages are served from staticAssetsIncrementalCache, shared navigation disables automatic prefetching to eliminate RSC prefetch loops, staging stays isolated behind X-Robots-Tag noindex headers, and 16 permanent 301 redirects preserve legacy Squarespace URLs.
sections.imageAlt: LifeSmart school eligibility enquiry form and structured impact metrics grid.

decisions.choice: OpenNext on Cloudflare Workers with static-assets incremental cache
decisions.why: Serves prerendered pages directly from Cloudflare Workers Assets without waking NextServer on GET requests while keeping Server Actions live for form POSTs.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires building with Webpack rather than Turbopack and disabling automatic link prefetch on shared chrome to stay well within Workers Free daily request quotas.

decisions.choice: Typed TypeScript modules and self-hosted WOFF2 fonts instead of a CMS or Google Fonts
decisions.why: Eliminates database/CMS runtime dependencies and third-party font requests while keeping copy changes type-checked and self-contained.
decisions.tradeoff: Copy edits require a git commit and deploy, and critical fonts needed explicit preload links because Webpack emitted an empty font manifest.

decisions.choice: Progressive-enhancement-first UI (Server Actions, native disclosures, CSS radio tabs)
decisions.why: Ensures school staff on locked-down networks or users without JavaScript can still open mobile menus, filter FAQs, expand research disclosures, and submit validated forms.
decisions.tradeoff: Client enhancements layer onto native form semantics rather than driving the entire flow through client-only state.

decisions.choice: Custom Playwright, axe-core, and token-contrast verification scripts
decisions.why: Verifies OpenNext static-cache hits, bounded RSC request counts, CSP headers, and WCAG 2.0/2.1 AA compliance across 1440px, 393px, and 320px viewports.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires maintaining custom Node/Playwright QA scripts alongside standard type-checking and linting.

caseStudy.outcome:
The v12 site replaced the legacy Squarespace deployment on lifesmartfinance.com (with www redirecting 301 to the apex) alongside a dedicated staging Worker at marketing-staging.lifesmartfinance.com.

Automated browser and accessibility checks passed across all 18 core routes (100 Lighthouse mobile accessibility, zero horizontal overflow, and verified Server Action error and honeypot handling). Post-cutover production verification after a Workers Free daily-quota block on 26 October, a few remaining high-res client assets, and final verification of the 29 October legal-audit routes remain noted follow-ups.

DoomScroll reproduces the loop with content that cannot upset anyone: endless facts, no algorithm, no outrage.

sections.title: The endless feed
sections.body:
Facts load continuously as you scroll, with no end state and nothing to complete.

React on the client with a small Node service supplying the stream.
sections.imageAlt: DoomScroll infinite feed of useless facts

decisions.choice: An endless client-side feed rather than pagination
decisions.why: Reproducing the never-ending scroll mechanic is the entire point of the project.
decisions.tradeoff: Memory and scroll performance need attention as the list grows.

decisions.choice: Harmless fact content
decisions.why: Parodying doomscrolling without the doom keeps it a joke rather than a habit.
decisions.tradeoff: No emotional pull — which is precisely the intent.

decisions.choice: A Node service on Render
decisions.why: Simple deploys for a low-traffic side project.
decisions.tradeoff: Free-tier cold starts.

caseStudy.outcome: Live at infinite-useless-scroll.onrender.com — a deliberately harmless infinite feed that never runs out of facts.

projects.name: Contrarian
projects.description: Pitchdeck classifier

caseStudy.claim: Pitch-deck classifier that turns inbound VC decks into scored, comparable screening rounds using ML and OpenAI.
caseStudy.role: Full-stack developer and data scientist
caseStudy.timeline: Contract, 2024–present · internal tool, not publicly hosted
caseStudy.problem:
A VC inbox receives far more decks than any partner can read, and the first pass is repetitive judgement work.

Contrarian had to turn an uploaded deck into a structured, comparable score rather than a gut reaction that varies by reviewer and by hour.

sections.title: Deck upload and classification
sections.body:
Decks are uploaded, parsed, and classified, with Firebase Storage holding the confidential files behind access rules.

A React UI keeps reviewers out of the Python tooling underneath.
sections.imageAlt: Contrarian pitch-deck upload and classification homepage

sections.title: Screening rounds
sections.body:
Decks progress through screening rounds so reviewers compare like with like instead of re-reading everything.

Flask serves the model output that drives each round.
sections.imageAlt: Contrarian second screening round with classified pitch decks

decisions.choice: ML classification plus an LLM pass
decisions.why: Structured features catch what a language model glosses over, and the model catches what the features miss.
decisions.tradeoff: Two systems to evaluate and keep calibrated against each other.

decisions.choice: A Python/Flask backend behind a React UI
decisions.why: The modelling work belongs in Python; reviewers need a fast web interface.
decisions.tradeoff: Separate deploys for the API and the client.

decisions.choice: Firebase Storage for uploaded decks
decisions.why: Decks are confidential files that need access-controlled storage.
decisions.tradeoff: Storage rules become part of the security surface.

caseStudy.outcome: Delivered an internal screening tool that ingests pitch decks, classifies them with ML and OpenAI, and presents scored rounds to reviewers — kept private rather than publicly hosted.

projects.name: Liberal Democrats
projects.description: Informative Website for the LDMF

caseStudy.claim: Campaign and policy site for the LDMF with a self-updating news feed aggregated from NewsAPI, MediaStack, and Google News.
caseStudy.role: Volunteer web developer

metrics.label: news sources aggregated: NewsAPI, MediaStack, Google News RSS

caseStudy.problem:
Campaign sites go stale between elections, and volunteers rarely have time to hand-write news updates.

The LDMF site needed clear policy pages plus a feed that keeps itself current with no editor in the loop.

sections.title: Policy and campaign pages
sections.body:
Positions on housing, education, equality, climate, and mental health each get a dedicated page written to be read, not skimmed past.

Built in Vue.js as static content that does not depend on any API being up.
sections.imageAlt: LDMF campaigns page listing policy positions

sections.title: Live news aggregation
sections.body:
Three sources — NewsAPI, MediaStack, and Google News RSS — feed a news page that stays current without a volunteer editing it.

Using three providers covers the gaps any single feed leaves.
sections.imageAlt: LDMF news page with aggregated live coverage

sections.title: Get involved
sections.body:
Join and contact routes turn a reader into a volunteer without leaving the site.

The conversion path was the point of the build.
sections.imageAlt: LDMF join us page with volunteer sign-up

decisions.choice: Aggregating three news sources instead of one
decisions.why: Single-feed coverage leaves visible gaps; three keep the page genuinely current.
decisions.tradeoff: De-duplication and inconsistent metadata across providers.

decisions.choice: Vue.js for the site
decisions.why: A small component-driven site with straightforward reactivity needs.
decisions.tradeoff: A different stack from the rest of the portfolio.

decisions.choice: Static policy pages alongside the dynamic feed
decisions.why: Positions change slowly and should not go blank when an API is down.

caseStudy.claim: Browser tool that traces uploaded PNGs into scalable SVG paths, with no install and no upload to a third party.
caseStudy.role: Sole developer
caseStudy.problem:
Raster logos fall apart the moment they are scaled up, and desktop tracing tools are overkill for a one-off conversion.

PNG to SVG does the trace in a browser tab, so a designer or developer can convert an asset without installing anything.

sections.title: Upload, trace, download
sections.body:
Drop in a PNG, trace it to vector paths, and download the resulting SVG.

The hosted free-tier instance was not returning a renderable page when this case study was captured, so it leads with a product card rather than a screenshot.
sections.imageAlt: PNG to SVG product card — browser-based raster-to-vector conversion utility

decisions.choice: Tracing in the browser
decisions.why: Uploaded artwork does not need to leave the machine for a vector trace.
decisions.tradeoff: Large images are limited by the device’s CPU.

decisions.choice: Angular for the tool shell
decisions.why: Built around Angular’s form and file-handling primitives for a self-contained utility.
decisions.tradeoff: A heavy framework for a single-purpose converter.

decisions.choice: Free-tier hosting on Render
decisions.why: The right cost for an occasional-use utility with no revenue.
decisions.tradeoff: Cold starts, and the instance can be unavailable between uses.

A Nuxt front end collects the questionnaire and a Flask service runs the matching against OpenAI.

caseStudy.role: Sole developer
caseStudy.problem:
Developer networking happens in crowded chat servers where introductions rarely turn into an actual conversation.

Tindev paired profile matching with a direct video call, so a match could become a conversation in one step instead of a dead DM.

Firebase-backed profiles drive matching and double as the WebRTC signalling channel for peer-to-peer video.

The prototype was never publicly deployed, so this case study uses a product card rather than a live capture.
sections.imageAlt: Tindev product card — developer networking prototype with matching and WebRTC video

projects.name: Stockfish Chess Studio
projects.description: A browser-based chess studio for players and teachers to compare Stockfish lines, replay games, and share positions for lessons.

caseStudy.claim: Compare Stockfish's strongest moves on the board and play through the ideas behind them.
caseStudy.role: Developer — chess studio, browser extension, and Cloudflare deployment setup.
caseStudy.timeline: October 2026 · web studio and browser extension
caseStudy.problem:
When teaching chess, you often need to pause at a position and ask what would happen if a player chose a different move. A useful lesson needs a board students can follow, candidate moves they can compare, and a way to return to the game.

Positions can come from a diagram, a saved game, or an analysis tab. The studio brings them onto one board so teachers and learners can explore the same position and share it for later study.

sections.title: Make engine lines playable
sections.body: I built an interactive board that puts Stockfish's best move, evaluation, and candidate lines beside the position. Players can adjust search depth and line count, compare the best move for either side, and click a candidate line to play its first move. Arrows show where those moves start and end.
sections.imageAlt: Light-mode chess studio showing a Ruy Lopez position, a best-move arrow for Re8, and three Stockfish lines.

sections.title: Bring a position to a lesson
sections.body: The studio accepts FEN positions and PGN games, and the board editor lets a teacher set up a position by hand. Students can open a shared position or game link. Move history makes it possible to return to an earlier decision, while PGN export includes the full game even when an earlier move is selected.
sections.imageAlt: Dark-mode studio with 7.Bb3 selected in the Ruy Lopez move history and the FEN and PGN fields visible below.

sections.title: Follow a board in a separate tab
sections.body: The browser extension lets users select a supported board in an analysis or replay tab and follow it in the studio. Exploring a variation pauses mirroring while the extension keeps capturing the source. Return to source restores the latest synchronized position. When a source provides only piece placement midgame, the user can supply missing turn and castling information to start the capture.
sections.imageAlt: Expanded Follow a board panel with instructions for connecting a browser tab and choosing a studio destination.

decisions.choice: Run Stockfish in a Web Worker
decisions.why: A lite WebAssembly build keeps analysis on the device and leaves the board responsive during search.
decisions.tradeoff: The single-threaded build has less search capacity than a full multithreaded engine.

decisions.choice: Share the studio between the website and extension
decisions.why: Both entry points offer the same board, engine controls, and study tools from one implementation.
decisions.tradeoff: Tab tracking still needs extension permissions and browser-specific packaging.

decisions.choice: Read a selected board and wait for stable snapshots
decisions.why: Users choose the source tab, and requiring two matching snapshots helps filter out transient states during moves and animations.
decisions.tradeoff: Mirroring has a short delay. Midgame captures can need manual position setup, and site markup changes can affect compatibility.

caseStudy.outcome:
The browser studio is live with on-device Stockfish analysis, a position editor, and FEN and PGN workflows. The Chromium extension is available as an unpacked build from the public source and can open the same studio or follow a supported analysis or replay board.

Use board tracking for study and replay where the source site's rules allow engine assistance. The repository documents limitations for canvas-only and video sources.

projects.name: Free Parking Finder
projects.description: A UK map of published on-street parking rules, so drivers can see what the kerb sign actually allows — free, paid, permit or banned.

caseStudy.claim: A UK parking map that only draws what a published sign or tag actually says — a blank road is not free parking.
caseStudy.role: Engineering contributor — parking data pipeline, rules engine, map UI, and Cloudflare deploy.
caseStudy.problem:
UK kerbside parking is split across hundreds of council portals, AppyWay snapshots and OpenStreetMap. Most products fill the gaps with a guess: an untagged road looks free, a controlled zone looks like a street, and the driver only finds out after a ticket.

Free Parking Finder takes the opposite position. A blank road is not free parking. A zone is never a free street. A missing OpenStreetMap tag is not drawn. The result is a UK-wide map that is honest about what it does not know, and fast enough to use at the kerb.

sections.title: A map that refuses to guess
sections.body:
Every surface — map paint, ranked list, 24-hour bay timeline, the "I'm parked here" countdown and the next-move reminder — is driven by one classifier, classifyParking. It runs on a Europe/London clock, with bank holidays resolved for England and Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland from the coordinate.

Zones are drawn as purple outlines, never painted as free streets. A bay beats a timed yellow line on the same kerb; a ban beats free; event-day and match-day clauses are stripped from everyday status and surfaced separately. If a council file has no rule for a kerb, the map stays silent instead of colouring it green.
sections.imageAlt: Free Parking Finder desktop view: a ranked list of 444 free bays in Belsize Park beside a street map with green free-parking kerb lines and bay callouts.

sections.title: UK-wide coverage without a 200 MB download
sections.body:
The national layer is 200,025 OpenStreetMap on-street features in 75 tiles, plus 74 council layers. Shipping all of that at startup would make the map unusable, so each GeoJSON file carries a bounding box in manifest.json. Core files load first; council and national tiles are fetched only when a search or the current view overlaps their box, with a spatial index and a 28-file cap keeping the loaded set small.

The same pipeline handles the awkward cases: kerb conflicts (a ban beats free on the same side of the road), free bays inside a zone (a note says the council data has no rule of its own, so check the sign), and shared-use Surrey bays whose text names no payment and no stay. QA fails if any kerb is both free and banned at any time.
sections.imageAlt: Zoomed map of Belsize Park showing green free bays, red suspension dots, and yellow and blue restriction lines along the kerbs.

sections.title: Plan the stay, not just the spot
sections.body:
Search a town, street, postcode or camera, or drop a pin. Results can be sorted by Closest, Fits stay, Longest free, or Cheapest where a council publishes a price. A Plan time control recomputes the list for a chosen arrival and stay, and preferences cover maximum walk, Blue Badge, motorcycle and EV needs in localStorage.

Opening a bay shows a 24-hour timeline, the next restriction, maximum stay, published tariff and permit code. "I'm parked here" starts a countdown, checks Camden's live suspension feed, warns about no-return limits, and can export a calendar reminder. Visited areas can be cached for patchy signal, and the service worker keeps the shell and parking files available offline.
sections.imageAlt: Bay card for Howitt Road with a 24-hour free and controlled timeline, next restriction time, maximum stay, Camden tariff and Open Government Licence attribution.

sections.title: A licence gate and a feedback loop
sections.body:
Coverage is gated by licence class. Class A (OGL, CC-BY, ODbL) may be added; class B (no terms stated) is allowed only with an on switch in EXTRA_PARKING and a rollback note; class C (view-only or no-copy) is never traced. Every council row can be switched off without a code change, and docs/ROLLBACK.md records each Cloudflare restore point.

Drivers can flag a kerb where the sign differs. The Worker writes the report and optional photo to D1 and R2 behind a rate limit, and /review lets a moderator confirm it with a bearer token. Reports are advisory: they never recolour a bay or change a published rule. The sign at the kerb still wins.
sections.imageAlt: Sign report form for flagging a kerbside sign that differs from the published parking rule, with the map point and optional photo field.

decisions.choice: Draw only what the source says
decisions.why: A driver acting on a green line needs the line to mean a published free bay, not an inference from a blank road or a zone polygon.
decisions.tradeoff: Visible gaps. Coverage is lower than commercial apps that infer, and some councils simply have no reusable file.

decisions.choice: One classifier behind every surface
decisions.why: The map, list, timeline, parking timer and next-move reminder must never disagree about whether a bay is free at 21:40 on a bank holiday.
decisions.tradeoff: classifyParking has to absorb every council wording quirk, event-day clause and DST edge case; a bug there shows up everywhere at once.

decisions.choice: Load layers by bounding box, not at startup
decisions.why: 552 MB of GeoJSON and 200,000 national features cannot be parsed on a phone before the first search.
decisions.tradeoff: A manifest to maintain, an extra fetch on first pan into a new area, and a cap on how many files stay loaded.

decisions.choice: Keep driver reports advisory
decisions.why: A user report is not a Traffic Regulation Order. Automatically rewriting a bay from a report would break the product's central promise.
decisions.tradeoff: A moderation queue, D1/R2 storage and spam limits, with no automatic correction loop.

caseStudy.outcome:
Free Parking Finder is live at https://freeparkingfinder.aden.website as v0.2.0. It covers Great Britain and Northern Ireland with 74 council layers and 200,025 OpenStreetMap on-street features, plus live car parks, EV chargers, taxi ranks and 3,541 speed cameras. Sign reports are switched on. The desktop layout, bay timeline, parking timer, offline cache and Camden suspension checks are all in the live build.

Two gaps are worth stating. The phone and landscape layout from pull request #11 (map above the list, bay card as a bottom sheet) is merged on master but was not in the live Worker as of 23 November 2026. Coverage is also bounded by reusable licences: D-TRO and the National Parking Platform are not on the map, several councils remain class B with per-file switches, and Northern Ireland has no council kerb file at all — only the national OSM layer.
